label: main_thm
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{main_thm}
	Let $T \colon \mathbf{X} \multimap \mathbf{X}^*$ be a set-valued operator on a separable Banach space $\mathbf{X}$. The following statement holds.
	\begin{enumerate}[ref=(\arabic*)]
		\item\label{main_thm_existence} \emph{(Existence)} $T$ is cyclically quasi-monotone if and only if $T \subseteq \mathrm{N} f$ for some $f \in \mathscr{Q}_0(\mathbf{X})$. Such an $f$ is called a quasi-convex potential of $T$.
	\end{enumerate}
	Moreover, if $\mathbf{X}$ is finite-dimensional, the following statements also hold.
	\begin{enumerate}[resume, ref=(\arabic*)]
		\item\label{main_thm_maximal_CQM} \emph{(Maximal cyclical quasi-monotonicity)} $T$ is maximal cyclically quasi-monotone if and only if $T = \mathrm{N} f$ for some $f \in \mathscr{E}_0(\mathbf{X})$.
		\item\label{main_thm_nonuniqueness} \emph{(Nonuniqueness)} In general, the quasi-convex potential of a maximal cyclically quasi-monotone operator is not unique, even up to composition with an increasing function.
		\item\label{main_thm_maximal_QM} \emph{(Maximal quasi-monotonicity)} For every $f \in \mathscr{E}_0(\mathbf{X})$, the operator $\mathrm{N} f$ is maximal quasi-monotone.
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: rmk_separability
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk_separability}
	The separability assumption, which is absent from Rockafellar's theorem, is necessary: there exists a cyclically quasi-monotone operator on a nonseparable Banach space that admits no potential (\Cref{prp_nonseparable_counterexample}). In a more general setting, that of smoothable Banach spaces (which include all reflexive and all separable ones), every cyclically quasi-monotone operator is contained in the normal cone operator $\mathrm{N}_\preceq$ of some lower semicontinuous quasi-convex preference relation $\preceq$ (\Cref{thm_chain}, see \labelcref{normal_cone_operator_preference} for the definition of $\mathrm{N}_\preceq$), but separability is needed to represent such a relation by a real-valued function (\Cref{cor_rader_separable}).
head: environment
name: Necessity of separability

label: rmk_nonuniqueness
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk_nonuniqueness}
	The failure of uniqueness is severe: even the family of sublevel sets of a potential is not determined by the operator (\Cref{example_non_uniqueness}), as already observed by Crouzeix, Eberhard and Ralph for pseudoconvex functions \cite[Example~6.2]{crouzeixConvexLevelSets2016}. A choice is literally made in the proof: it relies on the axiom of choice through the Arrow--Hansson theorem (\Cref{pre-order_extension}), a generalization of Szpilrajn's theorem, which extends any partial order to a total order, in a non-trivial way.
head: environment
name: Nonuniqueness

label: cor_afriat
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor_afriat}
	Let $\mathbf{X}$ be a separable Banach space and $\mathcal D \subseteq \mathbf{X} \times \mathbf{X}^*$ be an arbitrary data set. The following assertions are equivalent.
	\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
		\item $\mathcal D$ is \emph{rationalized in the strict sense} by a utility function $u \colon \mathbf{X} \to \mathbb{R}$, i.e., strictly cheaper bundles are strictly worse:
		\[\forall (x,p) \in \mathcal D,\ \forall y \in \mathbf{X}, \qquad \pair{p}{y} < \pair{p}{x} \implies u(y) < u(x).\]
		Moreover, $u$ can be chosen upper semicontinuous and quasi-concave, and also essentially non-satiated (meaning that every local maximizer of $u$ is a strict global maximizer) if $\mathbf{X}$ is finite-dimensional.
		\item $\mathcal D$ satisfies the following weakening of GARP, which we call the \emph{Quasi Axiom of Revealed Preference} (QARP): there is no cycle of strict direct revealed preferences, i.e., no $(x_0,p_0), \ldots, (x_{N-1},p_{N-1}) \in \mathcal D$ such that, setting $x_N \coloneqq x_0$, $\pair{p_k}{x_{k+1}} < \pair{p_k}{x_k}$ for every $k < N$.
	\end{enumerate}

name: Generalized Afriat theorem

label: thm_rader
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Rader

title: Remark
body_md:
The classical proof decomposes into two steps: first build a general function $f$ that satisfies \labelcref{potential_preference_relation_Rader}, then modify it to make it lower semicontinuous. For the first step, consider a countable basis $(O_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}^*}$ of open sets of $X$, and set for every closed subset $C \subseteq X$,
	\[g(C) = \sum_{n\geq 1, O_n \subseteq X\setminus C} 2^{-n} \qquad\text{and}\qquad f(x) = 1-g(C_\preceq(x)).\]

	The second step is not easy, and relies on Debreu's Open Gap Lemma. In \cite{depascaleRockafellarTheoremCyclically2025}, we followed the same two-step strategy in the metric setting: for the first step, we gave an explicit function in the case of quasi-convex preference relations, and for the second step, we used the \emph{sublevel-stable lower semicontinuous envelope}, which we introduced there. This envelope, which is defined by
	\[\hat f(x) = \inf \left\{ \liminf_{n\to +\infty} f(x_n') : x_n' \to x'\text{ and } f(x') = f(x)\right\},\]
is lower semicontinuous and still represents the same relation. This gives another proof of Rader's theorem, which is less general as it is restricted to separable metric spaces, but whose construction is more explicit.

label: cor_rader_separable
title: Corollary

label: rmk_countability
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk_countability}
	Notice that if \labelcref{potential_preference_relation_Rader} holds, then the chain $\mathcal C_\preceq$ admits an order-preserving indexation by a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, given by $C_\preceq(x) \mapsto f(x)$. It is therefore necessary for $\mathcal C_\preceq$ to have a cardinality at most that of $\mathbb{R}$. Even more than that, it is known that admitting such an indexation is equivalent to being \emph{order-separable}, which in our context means that there exists a countable subfamily $(C_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}} \subseteq \mathcal C_\preceq$ such that for every $C, C' \in \mathcal C_\preceq$ that satisfy $C \subsetneq C'$, there exists $n$ for which $C \subseteq C_n \subseteq C'$. The second countability assumption on $X$ guarantees that any chain of closed sets is order-separable.
head: environment
name: Necessity of a countability hypothesis

label: convex_chain_operator_CQM
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{convex_chain_operator_CQM}
	Let $\mathcal C$ be a chain of subsets of $\mathbf{X}$. Then $\mathrm{N}\mathcal C$, defined in \labelcref{normal_cone_operator_chain}, is cyclically quasi-monotone.
head: environment

label: ascending_path_convex_chain
title: Proof
body_md:
By contradiction, assume that there exists an $\mathrm{N}\mathcal C$-ascending cycle $x_0, \ldots, x_N = x_0$ with associated $\mathrm{N}\mathcal C$-ascending directions $x_0^*, \ldots, x^*_{N-1}$:
	\begin{equation}\label{ascending_path_convex_chain}
		\forall j < N, \quad \pair{x^*_j}{x_{j+1}-x_j} > 0.
	\end{equation}
	By definition of $\mathrm{N}\mathcal C$, for every $j < N$, $x^*_j \in \mathrm{N}_{C_j}(x_j)$ for some $C_j \in \mathcal C$, which implies that $x_j \in C_j$ (recall that $\mathrm{N}_C(x) = \emptyset$ when $x \notin C$). From \labelcref{ascending_path_convex_chain} we then deduce that $x_{j+1} \notin C_j$ for every $j < N$, and since $x_{j+1} \in C_{j+1}$ (with $C_N \coloneqq C_0$) and $\mathcal C$ is a chain, we obtain
	\[C_0 \subsetneq C_1 \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq C_{N-1} \subsetneq C_0,\]
	a contradiction.

label: lsc_regularization
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lsc_regularization}
	Let $\preceq$ be a preference relation on $\mathbf{X}$, and define the relation $\overline{\preceq}$ on $\mathbf{X}$ by
	\[x \mathrel{\overline{\preceq}} y \iff x \text{ belongs to every set } \operatorname{cl} C_\preceq(x'),\ x' \in \mathbf{X}, \text{ that contains } y.\]
	Then $\overline{\preceq}$ is a lower semicontinuous preference relation, which is quasi-convex if $\preceq$ is quasi-convex, and $\mathrm{N}_\preceq \subseteq \mathrm{N}_{\overline{\preceq}}$.
head: environment
name: Lower semicontinuous regularization

title: Proof
body_md:
The relation $\overline{\preceq}$ is reflexive and transitive, and for every $y \in \mathbf{X}$, its lower contour set $C_{\overline{\preceq}}(y)$ is the intersection of the elements of $\mathcal K \coloneqq \{\operatorname{cl} C_\preceq(x') : x' \in \mathbf{X}\}$ that contain $y$. The family $\mathcal K$ is a chain, as the family of the closures of the elements of the chain $\mathcal C_\preceq$, and intersections of subfamilies of a chain form a chain (if $\bigcap \mathcal A \not\subseteq \bigcap \mathcal B$, some $B \in \mathcal B$ is contained in every $A \in \mathcal A$, so that $\bigcap \mathcal B \subseteq \bigcap \mathcal A$). Therefore the lower contour sets of $\overline{\preceq}$ form a chain, and since $x \in C_{\overline{\preceq}}(x)$ for every $x$, the relation $\overline{\preceq}$ is total. These sets are closed, and convex if $\preceq$ is quasi-convex, since the closure of a convex set is convex. Finally, $y \in C_{\overline{\preceq}}(y) \subseteq \operatorname{cl} C_\preceq(y)$ and $(A-y)^\circ = (\operatorname{cl} A - y)^\circ$ for every set $A$, so that, by \labelcref{normal_cone_operator_preference},
	\[\mathrm{N}_\preceq(y) = \mathrm{N}_{\operatorname{cl} C_\preceq(y)}(y) \subseteq \mathrm{N}_{C_{\overline{\preceq}}(y)}(y) = \mathrm{N}_{\overline{\preceq}}(y). \qedhere\]

label: prp_nonseparable_counterexample
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prp_nonseparable_counterexample}
	There exists a cyclically quasi-monotone operator $T \colon \mathbf{X} \multimap \mathbf{X}^*$ on some nonseparable Banach space $\mathbf{X}$ such that $T \not\subseteq \mathrm{N} f$ for every quasi-convex function $f \colon \mathbf{X} \to \mathbb{R}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We consider the Hilbert space $\mathbf{X} = \ell^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ consisting of functions $x$ which are square-summable, i.e., $\sum_{t\in \mathbb{R}} \abs{x(t)}^2 < +\infty$ (or equivalently, square-integrable for the counting measure), equipped with the scalar product $\pair{x}{y} = \sum_t x(t) y(t)$. We denote by $(e_s)_{s\in \mathbb{R}}$ the canonical orthonormal basis and we set for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$,
	\[V_t = \operatorname{\overline{span}} \{ e_s : s < t\}, \qquad W_t = \operatorname{\overline{span}}\{e_s : s \leq t\}.\]
	These closed subspaces form a chain $\mathcal C \coloneqq \{V_t\}_{t\in \mathbb{R}} \cup \{W_t\}_{t\in \mathbb{R}}$, and we set $T = \mathrm{N} \mathcal C$, which is cyclically quasi-monotone by \Cref{convex_chain_operator_CQM}. We proceed by contradiction, assuming that $T \subseteq \mathrm{N} f$ for some quasi-convex function $f \colon \mathbf{X} \to \mathbb{R}$.

	First of all, the normal cones of the elements of $\mathcal C$ are explicit, since $\mathrm{N}_M(x) = M^\perp$ for any closed subspace $M$ and any $x \in M$. Let us compute $T(e_t)$. Notice that the subspaces in $\mathcal C$ that contain $e_t$ are exactly the $W_r$'s with $r \geq t$ and the $V_r$'s with $r > t$, and $W_t$ is the smallest one. This implies
	\[T(e_t) = \mathrm{N}\mathcal C(e_t) = \mathrm{N}_{W_t}(e_t) = W_t^\perp.\]
	Now set $v_t \coloneqq \sum_{n\geq 1} e^{-n} e_{t-1/n} \in V_t$ and compute $T(v_t)$. The subspaces in $\mathcal C$ that contain $v_t$ are all $W_r$'s for $r \geq t$ and all $V_r$'s for $r \geq t$, and $V_t$ is the smallest one. We get
	\[T(v_t) = \mathrm{N}\mathcal C(v_t) = \mathrm{N}_{V_t}(v_t) = V_t^\perp.\]

	Setting $V'_t \coloneqq \{f \leq f(v_t)\}$ and $W'_t \coloneqq \{f \leq f(e_t)\}$, the inclusion $T(v_t) \subseteq \mathrm{N} f(v_t) = (V'_t - v_t)^\circ$ yields
	\[V'_t - v_t \subseteq T(v_t)^\circ = V_t^{\perp\circ} = V_t^{\perp\perp} = V_t,\]
	thus $V'_t \subseteq V_t$ since $v_t \in V_t$, and similarly $W'_t \subseteq W_t$.

	Since $e_t \in W'_t$ and $e_t \notin V_t \supseteq V'_t$, and since the sublevel sets of $f$ are nested, we get $V'_t \subsetneq W'_t$. As a consequence $f(v_t) < f(e_t)$ and
	\[I_t \coloneqq (f(v_t), f(e_t))\]
	is a nonempty open interval of $\mathbb{R}$. If $s < t$, then $v_t \in V'_t$ but $v_t \notin W_s \supseteq W'_s$. Again, since the sublevel sets of $f$ are nested, we get $W'_s \subsetneq V'_t$, thus $f(e_s) \leq f(v_t)$. Therefore $\sup I_s \leq \inf I_t$. We conclude that $\{I_s\}_{s\in \mathbb{R}}$ is an uncountable disjoint family of open intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: this is impossible, hence no potential $f$ for $T$ may exist.

\label{strict_part}
	Let $T \colon \mathbf{X} \multimap \mathbf{X}^*$ be a cyclically quasi-monotone operator. Then $\prec_T$ is contained in the strict part of $\preceq_T$, i.e., the relation defined by ($x \preceq_T y$ and $y \not\preceq_T x$).

title: Proof
body_md: If $x \prec_T y$, then $x \preceq_T y$ by \Cref{transitivity_properties} \labelcref{item_strict_implies_large}, but $y \not\preceq_T x$, since otherwise \Cref{transitivity_properties} \labelcref{item_mixed_transitivity} would give $x \prec_T x$, contradicting \Cref{transitivity_properties} \labelcref{item_strict_pre-order}.

	Let $T \colon \mathbf{X} \multimap \mathbf{X}^*$ be a cyclically quasi-monotone operator. For every $x \in \mathbf{X}$, the set $C^T(x)$ is closed and convex.

label: existence_maximal_extension
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{existence_maximal_extension}
	Every cyclically quasi-monotone operator $T \colon \mathbf{X} \multimap \mathbf{X}^*$ admits a maximal cyclically quasi-monotone extension.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the set
	\[\{S : S \text{ is cyclically quasi-monotone and } T \subseteq S\},\]
	ordered by inclusion, which is nonempty since it contains $T$. If $(T_i)_{i \in I}$ is a nonempty chain in this set, then $\bigcup_{i\in I} T_i$ is a cyclically quasi-monotone extension of $T$, since a cycle involves finitely many points, hence is contained in some $T_i$. Thus this set is inductive and, by Zorn's lemma, it admits a maximal element.

label: F_equals_normal_cone
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first part is \cite[Proposition~2.17~(ii)]{depascaleRockafellarTheoremCyclically2025}, whose proof we recall for completeness. Let $x \in \mathbf{X}$ and $x^* \in T(x)$. If we had $\pair{x^*}{y-x} > 0$ for some $y \in C^T(x)$, then $x \prec_T y \preceq_T x$, which implies $x \prec_T x$ by \Cref{transitivity_properties}: a contradiction. Thus $\pair{x^*}{y-x} \leq 0$ for every $y \in C^T(x)$, which means that $x^* \in \mathrm{N}_{C^T(x)}(x)$, and \labelcref{F_included_normal_cone} is proved.

	Now assume that $T$ is maximal and let $x \in \mathbf{X}$. Since $S^T(x) \subseteq C^T(x)$, \labelcref{F_included_normal_cone} yields
	\[T(x) \subseteq \mathrm{N}_{C^T(x)}(x) \subseteq (S^T(x) - x)^\circ,\]
	so that it suffices to show $(S^T(x) - x)^\circ \subseteq T(x)$. Let $x^* \in (S^T(x) - x)^\circ$ and define $\tilde T$ by $\tilde T(y) = T(y)$ for $y \neq x$ and $\tilde T(x) = T(x) \cup\{x^*\}$. Let us show that $\tilde T$ is still cyclically quasi-monotone.

	By contradiction, assume that there exists a $\tilde T$-ascending cycle $x_0,x_1, \ldots, x_n = x_0$ with corresponding $x_i^* \in \tilde T(x_i)$ for every $i < n$. Let us assume that it has minimal length, i.e., $n \geq 2$ is minimal, so that $x_i \neq x_j$ for every $0 \leq i \neq j < n$. Since $T$ is cyclically quasi-monotone, necessarily one of the $(x_i,x_i^*)$ is equal to $(x,x^*)$, say $(x_0,x_0^*) = (x,x^*)$. By minimality of $n$, for every $1 \leq i < n$, we have $x_i \neq x$ and thus $x_i^* \in \tilde T(x_i) = T(x_i)$. This implies that $x_1 \prec_T x_n = x$, i.e., $x_1 \in S^T(x)$. But $\pair{x^*}{x_1-x} = \pair{x_0^*}{x_1-x_0} > 0$, which contradicts $x^* \in (S^T(x) - x)^\circ$.

	Therefore $\tilde T$ is cyclically quasi-monotone, and since $T \subseteq \tilde T$ and $T$ is maximal, we have $T = \tilde T$, which implies that $x^* \in T(x)$. We get the result since $x^*$ was an arbitrary element of $(S^T(x) - x)^\circ$.

label: convexity_stable_by_union
title: Lemma

label: separation_union_convex_sets
title: Proof
body_md:
Since convexity only involves pairs of points, it suffices to show that for every $x, x' \in A$, the set
	\[K \coloneqq C \cup C', \quad \text{where } C \coloneqq C^T(x) \text{ and } C' \coloneqq C^T(x'),\]
	is convex. Notice that $K$ is closed by \Cref{contour_sets_closed_convex}. Since an intersection of closed half-spaces is convex, it suffices to separate $K$ from any $y \notin K$ by a closed affine hyperplane, namely to find $v^* \in \mathbf{X}^*$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{separation_union_convex_sets}
		\sup_{z \in K} \pair{v^*}{z} < \pair{v^*}{y}.
	\end{equation}
	Let us fix $y \notin K$, an equivalent norm $\norm{\cdot}$ on $\mathbf{X}$ that is Gâteaux-differentiable on $\mathbf{X} \setminus \{0\}$, and denote by $\norm{\cdot}^*$ its dual norm on $\mathbf{X}^*$ and by $\norm{\cdot}'$ its derivative.

	\paragraph{Simple case: when a projection exists.} Assume first that there exists a projection of $y$ onto $K$, i.e., a point $p \in K$ such that
	\[\norm{p-y} = \inf_{z \in K} \norm{z-y},\]
	which is always the case if $\mathbf{X}$ is finite-dimensional, since $K$ is closed. We set $u^* \coloneqq \norm{\cdot}'(p-y)$, which is well defined since $p \neq y$, and satisfies $\pair{u^*}{p-y} = \norm{p-y} > 0$. If $p \in C$, then $p$ minimizes $\norm{\cdot - y}$ on the convex set $C \subseteq K$, so that by Fermat's rule $-u^* \in \mathrm{N}_C(p)$, and similarly with $C'$. We distinguish two cases, the case $p \in C' \setminus C$ being symmetric to the first one.

	\textit{Case $p \in C \setminus C'$.} We already know that $-u^* \in \mathrm{N}_C(p)$, i.e., $\pair{-u^*}{z-p} \leq 0$ for every $z \in C$, and it remains to show that the same holds for $z \in C'$. First notice that, since $C^T(p) \subseteq C$ because $p \in C$, \Cref{F_equals_normal_cone} yields
	\[-u^* \in \mathrm{N}_C(p) \subseteq \mathrm{N}_{C^T(p)}(p) = T(p).\]
	Assume by contradiction that $\pair{-u^*}{c'-p} > 0$ for some $c' \in C'$. Then $p \prec_T c'$, and since $c' \preceq_T x'$, \Cref{transitivity_properties} implies $p \prec_T x'$, hence $p \preceq_T x'$, i.e., $p \in C'$: a contradiction with $p \notin C'$. Thus $\pair{-u^*}{z-p} \leq 0$ for every $z \in C'$, hence for every $z \in K$.

	\textit{Case $p \in C \cap C'$.} Then $-u^* \in \mathrm{N}_C(p) \cap \mathrm{N}_{C'}(p)$, i.e., $\pair{-u^*}{z-p} \leq 0$ for every $z \in C \cup C' = K$.

	In both cases, $v^* \coloneqq -u^*$ satisfies
	\[\sup_{z \in K} \pair{v^*}{z} \leq \pair{v^*}{p} < \pair{v^*}{y},\]
	which is \labelcref{separation_union_convex_sets}.

	\paragraph{General case: without projection.} In general, the existence of a projection is not guaranteed, thus we resort to Ekeland's variational principle instead. We set $r \coloneqq \inf_{z \in K} \norm{z-y}$, which is positive since $K$ is closed and $y \notin K$. By Ekeland's variational principle applied to the function $\varphi \colon z \mapsto \norm{z-y} + \chi_K(z)$, for every $\varepsilon \in \mathopen]0,\varepsilon_0\mathclose[$ where $\varepsilon_0 \coloneqq 1/2$, there exists a point $p_\varepsilon \in K$ such that $\norm{p_\varepsilon-y} \leq r + \varepsilon$ and
	\begin{equation}\label{ekeland_minimizer}
		p_\varepsilon \in \operatorname{arg\,min}_{z \in \mathbf{X}} \norm{z-y} + \chi_K(z) + \varepsilon \norm{z-p_\varepsilon}.
	\end{equation}
	If $p_\varepsilon \in C$, since $C \subseteq K$, we also have
	\[p_\varepsilon \in \operatorname{arg\,min}_{z \in \mathbf{X}} \norm{z-y} + \chi_C(z) + \varepsilon \norm{z-p_\varepsilon}.\]
	This is a convex problem, thus by Fermat's rule and the sum rule (the qualification condition being satisfied because the norm is continuous), using the differentiability of the norm and the fact that $p_\varepsilon \neq y$, we get
	\begin{gather}
		0 \in \partial \norm{\cdot}(p_\varepsilon-y) + \partial \chi_C(p_\varepsilon) + \varepsilon\partial \norm{\cdot}(0),\notag\\
		\shortintertext{i.e.,}
		0 = u^*_\varepsilon + v^*_\varepsilon + \varepsilon w^*_\varepsilon \quad\text{where}\quad u^*_\varepsilon = \norm{\cdot}'(p_\varepsilon-y),\ v^*_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{N}_C(p_\varepsilon),\ \norm{w^*_\varepsilon}^* \leq 1.\notag
	\end{gather}
	Compared with the simple case, the direction $-u^*_\varepsilon$ is perturbed by the term $\varepsilon w^*_\varepsilon$, but $v^*_\varepsilon$ still separates $y$ from $p_\varepsilon$. Indeed, since $\norm{u^*_\varepsilon}^* = 1$ and $\pair{u^*_\varepsilon}{p_\varepsilon -y} = \norm{p_\varepsilon -y}$, we have
	\begin{equation} \label{v_near_direction_y_minus_projection}
		\begin{aligned}
			\pair{v^*_\varepsilon}{y-p_\varepsilon} &= \pair{u^*_\varepsilon}{p_\varepsilon -y} + \varepsilon \pair{w^*_\varepsilon}{p_\varepsilon -y}\\
			& \geq \norm{p_\varepsilon-y} - \varepsilon \norm{w^*_\varepsilon}^* \norm{p_\varepsilon-y}\\
			& \geq \frac{1}{2} \norm{p_\varepsilon-y} \geq \frac{r}{2} > 0.
		\end{aligned}
	\end{equation}
	Similarly, if $p_\varepsilon \in C'$, we get $0 = u^*_\varepsilon + \tilde v^*_\varepsilon + \varepsilon \tilde w^*_\varepsilon$ with $\tilde v^*_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{N}_{C'}(p_\varepsilon)$ and $\norm{\tilde w^*_\varepsilon}^* \leq 1$, and \labelcref{v_near_direction_y_minus_projection} holds with $\tilde v^*_\varepsilon$ instead of $v^*_\varepsilon$. We distinguish two cases.

	\textit{Case $p_\varepsilon \notin C \cap C'$ for some $\varepsilon \in \mathopen]0,\varepsilon_0\mathclose[$.} By symmetry, we may assume that $p_\varepsilon \in C \setminus C'$. The argument of the simple case applies with $p_\varepsilon$ and $v^*_\varepsilon$ instead of $p$ and $-u^*$. Indeed, $v^*_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{N}_C(p_\varepsilon) \subseteq \mathrm{N}_{C^T(p_\varepsilon)}(p_\varepsilon) = T(p_\varepsilon)$, and if $\pair{v^*_\varepsilon}{c'-p_\varepsilon} > 0$ for some $c' \in C'$, then $p_\varepsilon \prec_T c' \preceq_T x'$ yields $p_\varepsilon \prec_T x'$, hence $p_\varepsilon \in C'$: a contradiction. Hence, using \labelcref{v_near_direction_y_minus_projection},
	\[\sup_{z \in K} \pair{v^*_\varepsilon}{z} \leq \pair{v^*_\varepsilon}{p_\varepsilon} < \pair{v^*_\varepsilon}{y},\]
	and $v^* \coloneqq v^*_\varepsilon$ satisfies \labelcref{separation_union_convex_sets}.

	\textit{Case $p_\varepsilon \in C \cap C'$ for every $\varepsilon \in \mathopen]0,\varepsilon_0\mathclose[$.} In that case, the first-order optimality conditions on $C$ and on $C'$ both hold, i.e.,
	\[0 = u^*_\varepsilon + v^*_\varepsilon + \varepsilon w^*_\varepsilon = u^*_\varepsilon+\tilde v^*_\varepsilon+\varepsilon \tilde w^*_\varepsilon.\]
	Contrary to the simple case, we cannot conclude directly, since $v^*_\varepsilon$ and $\tilde v^*_\varepsilon$ may differ. This is where the differentiability of the norm plays a crucial role: since $u^*_\varepsilon$ is the same in both conditions, we get
	\begin{equation}\label{directions_alignment}
		\norm{v^*_\varepsilon-\tilde v^*_\varepsilon}^* = \varepsilon\norm{w^*_\varepsilon-\tilde w^*_\varepsilon}^* \leq 2\varepsilon.
	\end{equation}
	Since $\norm{v^*_\varepsilon}^* \leq \norm{u^*_\varepsilon}^* + \varepsilon \leq 2$, the family $(v^*_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon \in \mathopen]0,\varepsilon_0\mathclose[}$ is bounded and by the Banach--Alaoglu theorem, there exists a weak-$*$ limit $v^*$ along some subnet $(v^*_{\varepsilon_i})_{i \in I}$ such that $\varepsilon_i \to 0$ along $I$. By \labelcref{directions_alignment} we have at the same time $v^*_{\varepsilon_i} \rightharpoonup v^*$ and $\tilde v^*_{\varepsilon_i} \rightharpoonup v^*$ weakly-$*$ along $I$. Now let us show that $v^*$ satisfies \labelcref{separation_union_convex_sets}. Take $c \in K$, for example $c \in C$. By \labelcref{v_near_direction_y_minus_projection} and since $\pair{v^*_\varepsilon}{c-p_\varepsilon} \leq 0$, we have
	\[\pair{v^*_\varepsilon}{y-c} \geq \pair{v^*_\varepsilon}{y-p_\varepsilon} \geq \frac{r}{2}.\]
	Taking $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_i$ and passing to the limit along $i \in I$ yields $\pair{v^*}{y-c} \geq r/2$, and the same holds for $c \in C'$, using $\tilde v^*_{\varepsilon_i}$ instead of $v^*_{\varepsilon_i}$. We have shown that
	\[\sup_{z\in K} \pair{v^*}{z} \leq \pair{v^*}{y} - \frac{r}{2} < \pair{v^*}{y}. \qedhere\]

label: normality_strict_part
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{normality_strict_part}
	Let $T \colon \mathbf{X} \multimap \mathbf{X}^*$ be an operator and $\preceq$ be a preference relation on $\mathbf{X}$. The following assertions are equivalent.
	\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
		\item\label{item_normality} $T \subseteq \mathrm{N}_\preceq$.
		\item\label{item_strict_part} $\prec_T$ is contained in the strict part of $\preceq$, i.e., for every $x, y \in \mathbf{X}$,
		\[x \prec_T y \implies y \not\preceq x.\]
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume \labelcref{item_strict_part}, and let $x \in \mathbf{X}$, $x^* \in T(x)$ and $y \preceq x$. If we had $\pair{x^*}{y-x} > 0$, then $x \prec_T y$, hence $y 
ot\preceq x$ by \labelcref{item_strict_part}: a contradiction. Thus $x^* \in \mathrm{N}_{C_\preceq(x)}(x) = \mathrm{N}_\preceq(x)$ by \labelcref{normal_cone_operator_preference}, and \labelcref{item_normality} holds.

	Conversely, assume \labelcref{item_normality}, and let $x, y \in \mathbf{X}$ be such that $x \prec_T y$. Consider a $T$-ascending path $(x_0, \ldots, x_N)$ from $x$ to $y$, with $T$-ascending directions $(x_0^*, \ldots, x_{N-1}^*)$. For every $i \in \{0, \ldots, N-1\}$, since $x_i^* \in \mathrm{N}_\preceq(x_i) = \mathrm{N}_{C_\preceq(x_i)}(x_i)$ by \labelcref{item_normality} and $\pair{x_i^*}{x_{i+1}-x_i} > 0$, we have $x_{i+1} 
ot\preceq x_i$, hence $x_i \preceq x_{i+1}$ by totality. If we had $y \preceq x$, then $x_1 \preceq \cdots \preceq x_N = y \preceq x = x_0$ would give $x_1 \preceq x_0$ by transitivity: a contradiction. Thus $y 
ot\preceq x$, and \labelcref{item_strict_part} holds.

label: thm_chain
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm_chain}
	Let $T \colon \mathbf{X} \multimap \mathbf{X}^*$ be a cyclically quasi-monotone operator on a smoothable Banach space $\mathbf{X}$. Then there exists a lower semicontinuous quasi-convex preference relation $\preceq$ on $\mathbf{X}$ such that $T \subseteq \mathrm{N}_\preceq$.
head: environment
name: Existence of a preference relation

title: Proof
body_md:
First of all, up to replacing $T$ by a maximal extension, which is possible by \Cref{existence_maximal_extension}, we can assume $T$ to be maximal cyclically quasi-monotone. We then consider a total preorder $\preceq'$ that extends $\preceq_T$ and preserves its strict part, as given by \Cref{pre-order_extension}.

	Let us show that $\preceq'$ is quasi-convex. We claim that for every $x \in \mathbf{X}$,
	\begin{equation}\label{C_t_is_union_C}
		C_{\preceq'}(x) = \bigcup_{x' : x' \preceq' x} C^T(x').
	\end{equation}
	The inclusion $C_{\preceq'}(x) \subseteq \bigcup_{x' : x' \preceq' x} C^T(x')$ is trivial because $x' \in C^T(x')$ for every $x'$. For the converse inclusion, consider $x' \preceq' x$ and $z \in C^T(x')$, meaning $z \preceq_T x'$. Since $\preceq'$ extends $\preceq_T$, we deduce that $z\preceq' x'$, and by transitivity of $\preceq'$ we get $z \preceq' x$. We have proved \labelcref{C_t_is_union_C}, which implies by \Cref{convexity_stable_by_union} that $C_{\preceq'}(x)$ is convex, for every $x$.

	Now, since $\prec_T$ is contained in the strict part of $\preceq_T$ (\Cref{strict_part}), which is preserved by $\preceq'$, \Cref{normality_strict_part} yields $T \subseteq \mathrm{N}_{\preceq'}$.

	Finally, by \Cref{lsc_regularization}, the relation $\preceq \coloneqq \overline{\preceq'}$ is a lower semicontinuous quasi-convex preference relation, and $T \subseteq \mathrm{N}_{\preceq'} \subseteq \mathrm{N}_\preceq$.

label: stratification
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{stratification}
	Let $T \colon \mathbf{X} \multimap \mathbf{X}^*$ be a cyclically quasi-monotone operator on a smoothable Banach space $\mathbf{X}$. For every integer $k \geq 1$, the set $B_k(T)$ is contained in a closed affine subspace of $\mathbf{X}$ of codimension at least $k$. In particular, if $\mathbf{X}$ has finite dimension $d$, then $B_k(T)$ is contained in an affine subspace of dimension at most $d-k$.
head: environment
name: Stratification

title: Proof
body_md:
By \Cref{thm_chain}, there exists a preference relation $\preceq$ on $\mathbf{X}$ such that $T \subseteq \mathrm{N}_\preceq$, i.e., $T(x) \subseteq \mathrm{N}_{C_\preceq(x)}(x)$ for every $x \in \mathbf{X}$ by \labelcref{normal_cone_operator_preference}. Let $x \in B_k(T)$ and let $L_x \subseteq T(x)$ be a vector subspace of dimension $k$. For every $x^* \in L_x$ and every $y \in C_\preceq(x)$, we have $\pair{x^*}{y-x} = 0$ since $\pm x^* \in \mathrm{N}_{C_\preceq(x)}(x)$, thus $C_\preceq(x) \subseteq x + L_x^\perp$, which is a closed affine subspace of codimension $k$. As a consequence, the closed affine hull $E_x$ of $C_\preceq(x)$ has codimension at least $k$.

	Since the lower contour sets of $\preceq$ form a chain, so does the family $(E_x)_{x \in B_k(T)}$. If $B_k(T)$ is empty, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, pick $x_0 \in B_k(T)$ such that the codimension $c$ of $E_{x_0}$ is minimal. For every $x \in B_k(T)$, either $E_x \subseteq E_{x_0}$, or $E_{x_0} \subseteq E_x$, in which case the codimension of $E_x$ is at most $c$, hence equal to $c$ by minimality, so that $E_x = E_{x_0}$ as nested closed affine subspaces of the same finite codimension. In both cases $x \in E_x \subseteq E_{x_0}$, and we conclude that $B_k(T) \subseteq E_{x_0}$, a closed affine subspace of codimension $c \geq k$.

label: dfn_essential_non_satiation
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{dfn_essential_non_satiation}
	A quasi-convex function $f \colon \mathbf{X} \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ is said to be \emph{essentially non-satiated} if every local minimizer of $f$ in $\operatorname{dom} f$ is a strict global minimizer. In particular, if $f$ has a minimizer in $\operatorname{dom} f$, then it is unique.
head: environment
name: Essential non-satiation

label: rmk_non_satiation
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk_non_satiation}
	The terminology comes from economics, where a preference relation is \emph{locally non-satiated} if every neighborhood of every point contains a strictly preferred point \cite[Definition~3.B.3]{mascolellMicroeconomicTheory1995}. For a utility function, this means that it has no local maximizer, and for $f$, that it has no local minimizer. Essential non-satiation allows one exception, namely a unique global minimizer, which corresponds to a \emph{bliss point} in economics. In optimization, quasi-convex functions whose local minimizers in $\operatorname{dom} f$ are all global minimizers are called \emph{neatly quasi-convex} \cite[Proposition~4.1]{alhomidanTransformationQuasiconvexFunctions2018}. In \cite[Definition~4.1]{alhomidanTransformationQuasiconvexFunctions2018}, they are defined equivalently by the fact that $\{f < f(x)\}$ and $\{f \leq f(x)\}$ have the same closure, or the same relative interior, for every $x$ such that $f(x) > \inf f$. Thus $f$ is essentially non-satiated if and only if it is neatly quasi-convex and has at most one minimizer. Neat quasi-convexity is weaker than the classical \emph{semistrict quasi-convexity} \cite{karamardianStrictlyQuasiconvexConcave1967,avrielGeneralizedConcavity1988}, which requires $f(z) < f(y)$ for every $x, y \in \operatorname{dom} f$ such that $f(x) < f(y)$ and every $z \in \mathopen]x,y\mathclose[$. Both notions coincide for continuous functions \cite[Theorem~3.37]{avrielGeneralizedConcavity1988}, \cite[Proposition~4.2]{alhomidanTransformationQuasiconvexFunctions2018}, but not for lower semicontinuous ones \cite[Example~4.1]{alhomidanTransformationQuasiconvexFunctions2018}.

\label{equivalence_normal_cone_non_linear}
	Let $f \colon \mathbf{X} \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ be a quasi-convex function and $x \in \operatorname{dom} f$. Then $\mathrm{N} f(x)$ is a vector subspace of $\mathbf{X}^*$ if and only if $x \in \operatorname{ri} \{f \leq f(x)\}$.

title: Proof
body_md: Setting $K \coloneqq \{f \leq f(x)\}-x$ and $C \coloneqq \operatorname{\overline{cone}} K$, we have $\mathrm{N} f(x) = K^\circ = C^\circ$. Since $C$ is a closed convex cone, we have $C = C^{\circ\circ}$, and since the polar cone of a vector subspace is its orthogonal, $C$ is a vector subspace if and only if $C^\circ$ is. label: characterization_essential_non-satiation
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{characterization_essential_non-satiation}
	A quasi-convex function $f$ is essentially non-satiated if and only if for every $x \in \operatorname{dom} f$, $\mathrm{N} f(x)$ is not a proper vector subspace of $\mathbf{X}^*$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that $f$ is essentially non-satiated. In particular, $f$ admits at most one minimizer, thus
	\[x \text{ is a global minimizer } \iff x \text{ is a strict global minimizer } \iff \mathrm{N} f(x) = \mathbf{X}^*.\]
	It suffices to show that for any point $x$ which is not a global minimizer, $\mathrm{N} f(x)$ is not a vector subspace of $\mathbf{X}^*$. By \Cref{equivalence_normal_cone_non_linear}, this is equivalent to $x \notin \operatorname{ri} \{f \leq f(x)\}$. Assume by contradiction that for some $x$ which is not a minimizer of $f$, we have $x \in \operatorname{ri} \{f \leq f(x)\}$. This does not imply that $x$ is a local minimizer of $f$, but we show that there exists a point $x'$ such that $f(x') = f(x)$ and $x'$ is a local minimizer of $f$. Since in finite dimension we may always separate two disjoint convex sets by a linear form (in the weak sense), we may separate $x$ and $\{f < f(x)\}$ linearly in the affine span $A$ of $\{f \leq f(x)\}$, and extending the corresponding linear form to an element of $\mathbf{X}^*$ we obtain a linear form $x^* \in \mathbf{X}^*$ such that
	\[\sup_{y\in \{f < f(x)\}} \pair{x^*}{y-x} \leq 0\]
	and $x^*$ is not identically $0$ on $\{f \leq f(x)\}-x$. Since $x \in \operatorname{ri} \{f \leq f(x)\}$, we see that $H_+ \coloneqq \{y : \pair{x^*}{y-x} > 0\}$ has a nonempty intersection with $\{f \leq f(x)\}$ (just take $y = x+tu$ for $t > 0$ small and $\pair{x^*}{u} > 0$ for some well-chosen $u$ in the linear span of $\{f \leq f(x)\}-x$). By definition of $x^*$, we have $f \geq f(x)$ on the open set $H_+$. Consequently, any point $x' \in H_+ \cap \{f \leq f(x)\}$ satisfies $f(x') = f(x)$, and it is a local minimizer of $f$, since $f \geq f(x')$ on its open neighborhood $H_+$. Since $f(x') = f(x)$ and $x$ was assumed not to be a global minimizer, then $x'$ is not a global minimizer either, contradicting the fact that $f$ is essentially non-satiated.

	Conversely, assume that $\mathrm{N} f(x)$ is never a proper vector subspace of $\mathbf{X}^*$, and let $x \in \operatorname{dom} f$ be a local minimizer of $f$. Setting $C \coloneqq \{f \leq f(x)\}$, there exists $r > 0$ such that $f = f(x)$ on $C \cap B(x,r)$. By \Cref{relative_interior} \labelcref{item_ri_dense}, there exists $y \in \operatorname{ri} C \cap B(x,r)$. Then $f(y) = f(x)$, thus $\{f \leq f(y)\} = C$ and $y \in \operatorname{ri} \{f \leq f(y)\}$, so that $\mathrm{N} f(y)$ is a vector subspace by \Cref{equivalence_normal_cone_non_linear}. By assumption, $\mathrm{N} f(y) = \mathbf{X}^*$, i.e., $y$ is a strict global minimizer of $f$, so that $x = y$ is also a strict global minimizer of $f$, and $f$ is essentially non-satiated.

label: lem_equality_cones
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Notice that $S^{\mathrm{N} f}_1(x) \subseteq S^{\mathrm{N} f}(x) \subseteq \{f < f(x)\} \subseteq \{f \leq f(x)\}$. Besides, since $\{f \leq f(x)\}$ is nonempty, closed and convex, \Cref{relative_interior} \labelcref{item_ri_dense} yields
	\[\operatorname{cl} \operatorname{ri} \{f \leq f(x)\} = \{f \leq f(x)\}.\]
	To get the equalities of all considered cones, it thus suffices to show that
	\[\operatorname{ri} \{f \leq f(x)\}-x \subseteq \operatorname{\overline{cone}} (S^{\mathrm{N} f}_1(x)-x).\]

	The essential non-satiation of $f$ guarantees that
	\[\operatorname{ri} \{f \leq f(x)\} \subseteq \{f < f(x)\}.\]
	Indeed, by contraposition, if $y$ is a point such that $f(y) = f(x)$, then by \Cref{characterization_essential_non-satiation} and the fact that $x$ is not a minimizer of $f$ (hence neither is $y$), $\mathrm{N} f(y)$ is not a vector subspace of $\mathbf{X}^*$, and by \Cref{equivalence_normal_cone_non_linear} it implies that $y \notin \operatorname{ri} \{f \leq f(x)\}$. In other words, $\{f < f(x)\}$ and $\{f \leq f(x)\}$ have the same relative interior (see \cite[Proposition~4.1]{alhomidanTransformationQuasiconvexFunctions2018} and \Cref{rmk_non_satiation}).

	Let us show that for every $y \in \operatorname{ri} \{f \leq f(x)\}$, for $t > 0$ small enough we have $x+t(y-x) \in S^{\mathrm{N} f}_1(x)$. By contradiction, assume that $x_n \coloneqq x+t_n(y-x) \notin S^{\mathrm{N} f}_1(x)$ for some sequence $t_n \downarrow 0$. Since $f$ is lower semicontinuous and $x_n \to x$, we get $f(x) \leq \liminf_n f(x_n)$. But $x_n$ lies on the segment between $x \in \{f \leq f(x)\}$ and $y \in \operatorname{ri} \{f \leq f(x)\}$, so that $x_n \in \operatorname{ri} \{f \leq f(x)\} \subseteq \{f < f(x)\}$ for every $n$, and thus $f(x_n) \to f(x)$. Therefore
	\begin{equation}\label{union_strict_sublevels}
		\{f < f(x)\} = \bigcup_{n\in \mathbb{N}} \{f \leq f(x_n)\}.
	\end{equation}
	By \labelcref{union_strict_sublevels} and the fact that $\{f < f(x)\}$ is dense in $\{f \leq f(x)\}$, the affine span of $\{f \leq f(x_n)\}$ coincides with that of $\{f \leq f(x)\}$ for $n$ large enough, which we assume from now on. Denoting by $V$ the direction of this affine span, we get $\operatorname{lin} \mathrm{N} f(x_n) = (\{f \leq f(x_n)\}-x_n)^\perp = V^\perp$.

	For every $n$, since $x_n$ is not a minimizer of $f$, the cone $\mathrm{N} f(x_n)$ is not a vector subspace by \Cref{characterization_essential_non-satiation}, hence it contains some $y_n^* \notin V^\perp$. Let $p_n$ be a closest point to $y_n^*$ in $V^\perp$. Since $-p_n \in V^\perp = \operatorname{lin} \mathrm{N} f(x_n)$, the linear form $y_n^* - p_n$ still belongs to $\mathrm{N} f(x_n)$, and $\operatorname{dist}(y_n^* - p_n, V^\perp) = \operatorname{dist}(y_n^*, V^\perp) = \norm{y_n^* - p_n} > 0$. Dividing by this quantity, we obtain $x_n^* \in \mathrm{N} f(x_n)$ such that $\norm{x_n^*} = \operatorname{dist}(x_n^*, V^\perp) = 1$. From $x_n \notin S^{\mathrm{N} f}_1(x)$ we obtain $\pair{x_n^*}{x-x_n} \leq 0$, or equivalently
	\[\pair{x_n^*}{y-x} \geq 0.\]
	Besides, since $f(y) < f(x) = \lim_n f(x_n)$ we know that for $n$ large enough $y \in \{f \leq f(x_n)\}$, thus $\pair{x_n^*}{y-x_n} \leq 0$, or equivalently
	\[ \pair{x_n^*}{y-x} \leq 0.\]
	As a consequence $\pair{x_n^*}{y-x} = 0$ for every $n$ large enough. By relative compactness of bounded subsets in finite dimension, we can extract a subsequence (relabeled) $(x_n^*)$ which converges to some $x^*$ such that $\operatorname{dist}(x^*, V^\perp) = 1$, and which still satisfies
	\[\pair{x^*}{y-x} = 0.\]
	Besides, $x_n^*$ being in $\mathrm{N} f(x_n)$ we have $\pair{x_n^*}{z-x_n} \leq 0$ for every $z$ in $\{f \leq f(x_n)\}$ thus for every $z \in \{f < f(x)\}$ for $n$ large enough, and by passing to the limit we get
	\[\forall z \in \{f < f(x)\}, \quad \pair{x^*}{z-x} \leq 0.\]
	By density of $\operatorname{ri} \{f \leq f(x)\}$, thus of $\{f < f(x)\}$, in $\{f \leq f(x)\}$, it means that $x^* \in \mathrm{N} f(x)$. We therefore get a contradiction: since $\pair{x^*}{y-x} = 0$, $x^*$ attains its maximum on $\{f \leq f(x)\}$ at $x$ but also at $y$, and $y$ is a relative interior point of $\{f \leq f(x)\}$, thus $x^*$ is constant on that set, which means that $x^* \in V^\perp$, contradicting $\operatorname{dist}(x^*, V^\perp) = 1$.

label: thm_characterization_maximal
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm_characterization_maximal}
	Let $f \colon \mathbf{X} \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ be a proper lower semicontinuous quasi-convex function. The following assertions are equivalent.
	\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
		\item $\mathrm{N} f$ is maximal quasi-monotone.
		\item $\mathrm{N} f$ is maximal cyclically quasi-monotone.
		\item $f$ is real-valued and essentially non-satiated.
	\end{enumerate}

	Moreover, if $T$ is a cyclically quasi-monotone operator, the following assertions are equivalent.
	\begin{enumerate}[(i')]
		\item $T$ is maximal quasi-monotone.
		\item $T$ is maximal cyclically quasi-monotone.
		\item $T = \mathrm{N} f$ for some $f \in \mathscr{E}_0(\mathbf{X})$.
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Characterization of maximal operators

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\mathrm{N} f$ is maximal quasi-monotone, then it is maximal cyclically quasi-monotone, since it is cyclically quasi-monotone (\Cref{convex_chain_operator_CQM}) and cyclically quasi-monotone operators are quasi-monotone. If $\mathrm{N} f$ is maximal cyclically quasi-monotone, then $0 \in \mathrm{N} f(x)$ for every $x \in \mathbf{X}$, since adding $(x,0)$ to $\mathrm{N} f$ preserves cyclical quasi-monotonicity. Thus $f$ is real-valued, since $\mathrm{N} f(x) = \emptyset$ whenever $f(x) = +\infty$. Moreover, $\mathrm{N} f(x)$ is never a proper vector subspace of $\mathbf{X}^*$ by \Cref{values_maximal_operators}, which means that $f$ is essentially non-satiated by \Cref{characterization_essential_non-satiation}.

	Now assume that $f$ is real-valued and essentially non-satiated, and let $x \in \mathbf{X}$ and $x^* \in \mathbf{X}^*$ be such that $\mathrm{N} f \cup \{(x,x^*)\}$ is quasi-monotone. Then $\pair{x^*}{y-x} \leq 0$ for every $y \in S^{\mathrm{N} f}_1(x)$, i.e., $x^* \in (S^{\mathrm{N} f}_1(x)-x)^\circ$. If $x$ is the minimizer of $f$, then $\mathrm{N} f(x) = \mathbf{X}^*$ contains $x^*$. Otherwise, \Cref{lem_equality_cones} yields
	\[(S^{\mathrm{N} f}_1(x)-x)^\circ = (\{f \leq f(x)\}-x)^\circ = \mathrm{N} f(x),\]
	thus $x^* \in \mathrm{N} f(x)$. We have shown that $\mathrm{N} f$ is maximal quasi-monotone.
	
	Now let $T$ be a cyclically quasi-monotone operator. If $T$ is maximal quasi-monotone, then it is maximal cyclically quasi-monotone, since cyclically quasi-monotone operators are quasi-monotone. If $T$ is maximal cyclically quasi-monotone, then $T \subseteq \mathrm{N} f$ for some $f \in \mathscr{Q}_0(\mathbf{X})$ by item~\labelcref{main_thm_existence} of \Cref{main_thm}, and $T = \mathrm{N} f$ by maximality, since $\mathrm{N} f$ is cyclically quasi-monotone (\Cref{convex_chain_operator_CQM}). Then $f \in \mathscr{E}_0(\mathbf{X})$ by the implication (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii). Finally, if $T = \mathrm{N} f$ for some $f \in \mathscr{E}_0(\mathbf{X})$, then $T$ is maximal quasi-monotone by the implication (iii) $\Rightarrow$ (i), which ends the proof.

label: example_non_uniqueness
title: Example
body_md:
\label{example_non_uniqueness}
	Consider on $\mathbb{R}$ the functions $f_1(x) \coloneqq \abs{x}$ and
	\[
		f_2(x) \coloneqq
		\begin{cases}
			-x & \text{if } x \leq 0,\\
			2x & \text{if } x \geq 0.
		\end{cases}
	\]
	Both belong to $\mathscr{E}_0(\mathbb{R})$: they are continuous and quasi-convex, and $0$ is their only local minimizer, which is a strict global minimizer. For $t \geq 0$, their sublevel sets are $\{f_1 \leq t\} = [-t, t]$ and $\{f_2 \leq t\} = [-t, t/2]$. Hence, for every $x \in \mathbb{R}$,
	\[
		\mathrm{N} f_1(x) = \mathrm{N} f_2(x) =
		\begin{cases}
			[0, +\infty\mathclose[ & \text{if } x > 0,\\
			\mathbb{R} & \text{if } x = 0,\\
			\mathopen]-\infty, 0] & \text{if } x < 0.
		\end{cases}
	\]
	By \Cref{thm_characterization_maximal}, the operator $T \coloneqq \mathrm{N} f_1 = \mathrm{N} f_2$ is maximal cyclically quasi-monotone, and it admits two potentials whose families of sublevel sets, $\{[-t, t]\}_{t \geq 0}$ and $\{[-t, t/2]\}_{t \geq 0}$, differ. In particular, $f_2$ is not of the form $\varphi \circ f_1$ with $\varphi$ increasing.

label: infinite_CM_implies_CQM
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{infinite_CM_implies_CQM}
	Let $c(x,y) = -\pair{x}{y}$ and let $\Gamma \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d$ satisfy \eqref{infinite_cyclical_monotonicity} for every $(x_0,y_0), \ldots, (x_{N-1},y_{N-1}) \in \Gamma$. Then the operator $x \mapsto \{y \in \mathbb{R}^d : (x,y) \in \Gamma\}$ is cyclically quasi-monotone.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $(x_0,y_0), \ldots, (x_{N-1},y_{N-1}) \in \Gamma$ and set $x_N \coloneqq x_0$. Changing signs in \eqref{infinite_cyclical_monotonicity}, and since the minimum of a sum is at least the sum of the minima, we get
	\[
		\min_{0 \leq i < N} \pair{y_i}{x_i} \geq \min_{0 \leq i < N} \bigl(\pair{y_i}{x_i} + \pair{y_i}{x_{i+1}-x_i}\bigr) \geq \min_{0 \leq i < N} \pair{y_i}{x_i} + \min_{0 \leq i < N} \pair{y_i}{x_{i+1}-x_i}.
	\]
	Hence $\min_i \pair{y_i}{x_{i+1}-x_i} \leq 0$, which is \eqref{cyclical_quasi_monotonicity}.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm_supremal_OT}
	Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be Borel probability measures on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with compact supports, and let $c(x,y) = -\pair{x}{y}$. Then the following statements hold.
	\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
		\item The supremal optimal transport problem \eqref{Linfty_OT_problem} admits a restrictable solution.
		\item For every restrictable solution $\gamma$ of \eqref{Linfty_OT_problem}, there exists an essentially non-satiated function $f \in \mathscr{E}_0(\mathbb{R}^d)$ such that
		\[
			y \in \mathrm{N} f(x) \qquad \text{for every } (x,y) \in \operatorname{supp} \gamma.
		\]
	\end{enumerate}
